column38: I often run into stale dependencies, unclear setup assumptions, and templates that work well for the original use case but become brittle once adapted. The hardest part is usually maintenance: keeping the template updated without forcing downstream projects to manually reconcile changes or undo local customization.
column40: Make templates explicit about their intended use cases, setup assumptions, supported options, and what users are expected to customize. Add CI that validates a freshly generated project, automated dependency/security updates, and a clear upgrade path so downstream repos can adopt template improvements without painful manual diffs.

column40: GitHub could improve template repositories by providing better visibility for maintenance status, last updates, and compatibility information. Templates should include clear documentation, examples, automated dependency updates, and basic CI checks. It would also be useful to have better tools for tracking improvements made by users who create repositories from templates.
column42: Template repositories are very useful for quickly starting new projects and sharing best practices. However, their value depends heavily on active maintenance and good documentation. column40:
Nowadays folks go ahead use agentic coding, vibe coding and context engineering using agentic coding tools without a care in a world. They don't read most of the code or verify whether the data structures in use or the algorithms (which are rare in case of templates) are written in a scalable manner. All of my templates that I've created are from a time when vibe coding wasn't around. So I've coded every single line myself, with minor assistance with GitHub Co-pilot's inline coding assistance, so I've obviously read every single line of my code and know how it works and have no doubts in how it's supposed to work. In case of building GitHub template repositories in today's date and time, you will be using agentic coding tools, there's no denying that. We're way past the point of AI vs no AI for coding and there's no denying that it makes the development process much smoother, so two things need to be kept in mind:

1. You know how to write the entire thing yourself so that you can verify every line of code.
2. You NEED to verify every line of code.

Because, if the template has loopholes, your skyscraper, and God forbid, someone else's skyscraper is gonna take a deep dive.
column42: The motivation behind a GitHub template repository in my opinion should be to build something that you're doing often anyways. There's no point in doing the same thing again and again. Martin Fowler's rule of three is a great rule of thumb to follow which inspierd me to create template for my own use cases due to which I ended up creating multiple templates because I'm used to building microservices and APIs and it came quite in handy for me. If there's a certain structure you're following for buildling a certain type of project and you're doing the same thing for the third time, it's time you consider templating it.
